Physiology-02.question: ১) VC+RV=?
২) Vasogenic shock excludes
৩) Normal quiet breathing is accomplished almost entirely by movement of the
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Diaphragm. Normal quiet inspiration is accomplished mainly by contraction and downward movement of the diaphragm.

Mechanism:

  • Diaphragm contracts → moves downward

  • Thoracic volume increases

  • Intrapulmonary pressure decreases

  • Air enters the lungs

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Internal intercostal muscle ✗ → Mainly involved in forced expiration.

  • External intercostal muscle ✗ → Helps quiet inspiration by elevating ribs, but contributes less than the diaphragm.

  • Rectus abdominis ✗ → An accessory muscle of forced expiration.

High-yield Respiratory recall:

Breathing type Main muscle
Quiet inspiration Diaphragm
Forced inspiration External intercostals + accessory muscles
Forced expiration Internal intercostals + abdominal muscles

Exam pearl:
Diaphragm is the principal muscle of normal quiet breathing.

Physiology-02.question: ৪) Which one is called pacemaker of heart?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is SA node (Sinoatrial node). The SA node is called the pacemaker of the heart because it has the highest rate of spontaneous depolarization and initiates normal cardiac rhythm.

Key points:

  • Location: Right atrium near the opening of superior vena cava

  • Intrinsic firing rate: ~60–100 beats/min

  • Generates the normal cardiac impulse

The other options are incorrect because:

  • AV node ✗ → Delays conduction between atria and ventricles; backup pacemaker (~40–60/min).

  • Bundle of His ✗ → Conducts impulses from AV node to ventricular conduction system.

  • Purkinje fibres ✗ → Spread impulses through ventricles; slow intrinsic rhythm (~20–40/min).

High-yield Cardiac physiology recall:

Structure Function Rate
SA node Primary pacemaker 60–100/min
AV node Conduction delay 40–60/min
Purkinje fibres Ventricular conduction 20–40/min

Exam pearl:
SA node = natural pacemaker of the heart.

Physiology-02.question: ৫) At a normal heart rate, the duration(second) of ventricular systole is
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is 0.3 second. At a normal heart rate, ventricular systole lasts approximately 0.3 seconds.

Duration of cardiac cycle (HR ≈ 75/min):

  • Total cardiac cycle → 0.8 sec

  • Atrial systole → 0.1 sec

  • Ventricular systole → 0.3 sec

  • Complete diastole → 0.4 sec

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 0.1 sec ✗ → Duration of atrial systole.

  • 0.5 sec ✗ → Not the normal duration of ventricular systole.

  • 0.7 sec ✗ → Longer than a normal cardiac cycle phase.

High-yield Cardiac physiology recall:

Event Duration
Atrial systole 0.1 sec
Ventricular systole 0.3 sec
Diastole 0.4 sec
Cardiac cycle 0.8 sec

Exam pearl:
Ventricular systole = 0.3 second at normal heart rate.

Physiology-02.question: ৬) The normal dead space air in a young man is about ... ml
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is 150 ml. Normal anatomical dead space (air that does not participate in gas exchange) is approximately 150 mL in a healthy young adult.

Dead space:

  • Located in conducting airways:

    • Nose

    • Trachea

    • Bronchi

  • No alveolar gas exchange occurs here.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 100 ml ✗ → Lower than the normal adult value.

  • 200 ml ✗ → Higher than normal anatomical dead space.

  • 250 ml ✗ → Not the usual physiological value.

High-yield Respiratory recall:

Parameter Value
Anatomical dead space ~150 ml
Tidal volume ~500 ml
Alveolar ventilation TV − dead space = 500 − 150 = ~350 ml/breath

Exam pearl:
Dead space = 150 ml; tidal volume = 500 ml in a normal adult.

Physiology-02.question: ৭) Which initiates cardiac cycle
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Atrial systole. The cardiac cycle is considered to begin with atrial systole, which follows the initiation of the electrical impulse from the SA node and atrial contraction.

Sequence of cardiac cycle:

  1. Atrial systole → atria contract and complete ventricular filling

  2. Ventricular systole → ventricles contract and eject blood

  3. Ventricular diastole → ventricles relax and fill

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Atrial diastole ✗ → Relaxation phase of atria, not the starting phase.

  • Ventricular systole ✗ → Occurs after atrial contraction.

  • Ventricular diastole ✗ → Filling phase after ventricular contraction.

High-yield Cardiac physiology recall:

Phase Duration
Atrial systole 0.1 sec
Ventricular systole 0.3 sec
Diastole 0.4 sec

Exam pearl:
Cardiac cycle starts with atrial systole (after SA node discharge).

Physiology-02.question: ৮) Tidal volume in women
৯) Ejection click occurs following which heart sound?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is 2nd heart sound (S2). An ejection click occurs immediately after S2 during early systole, usually due to abnormal opening of semilunar valves.

Causes of ejection click:

  • Bicuspid (bileaflet) aortic valve

  • Pulmonary valve stenosis

  • Dilated aortic root or pulmonary artery

Heart sound timing:

  • S1 → Closure of mitral and tricuspid valves (start of systole)

  • S2 → Closure of aortic and pulmonary valves (end of systole)

  • Ejection click → Shortly after S2 (early systolic click)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 1st heart sound ✗ → Associated with AV valve closure; followed by systole.

  • 3rd heart sound ✗ → Occurs during rapid ventricular filling in diastole.

  • 4th heart sound ✗ → Occurs during atrial contraction.

High-yield Cardiac auscultation recall:

Sound Timing
S1 Beginning of systole
S2 End of systole
Ejection click Shortly after S2
S3 Early diastole
S4 Late diastole

Exam pearl:
Ejection click = early systolic sound, classically just after S2.

Physiology-02.question: ১০) Effect of exercise on cardiac output excludes
Physiology-02.option3: Decrease venous return and thus stroke volume
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Decrease venous return and thus stroke volume. During exercise, venous return increases due to muscle pump and sympathetic stimulation, which increases stroke volume and cardiac output.

Effects of exercise on cardiac output:

  • Positive chronotropism ✓
    → Increased heart rate

  • Positive inotropism ✓
    → Increased myocardial contractility

  • Increase venous return and stroke volume ✓
    → Due to skeletal muscle pump and venoconstriction

  • Decrease in total peripheral resistance ✓
    → Due to vasodilation in active skeletal muscles

The other options are correct effects of exercise.

High-yield Cardiac physiology recall:

Exercise → ↑ Cardiac output

Mechanisms:

  • ↑ Heart rate (positive chronotropy)

  • ↑ Contractility (positive inotropy)

  • ↑ Venous return → ↑ Stroke volume

  • ↓ Total peripheral resistance

Exam pearl:
Exercise increases venous return, not decreases it.

Physiology-02.question: ১১) Maximum percentage of 02 is present in
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Atmospheric air. Atmospheric (dry) air contains the highest percentage of oxygen (~21%) compared with other forms of air in the respiratory system.

Approximate oxygen concentration:

Type of air Oxygen (%)
Atmospheric air ~21%
Humidified air ~20.9% (slightly reduced due to water vapour)
Alveolar air ~13–14%
Expired air ~16%

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Humidified air ✗ → Water vapour dilutes oxygen slightly.

  • Alveolar air ✗ → Oxygen decreases due to continuous uptake into blood.

  • Expired air ✗ → Contains less oxygen after gas exchange.

High-yield Respiratory recall:

O₂ concentration:
Atmospheric air (21%) > Expired air (16%) > Alveolar air (13–14%)

Exam pearl:
Maximum oxygen percentage is present in atmospheric air.

Physiology-02.question: ১২) Which is not a part of Respiratory Unit (also called respiratory lobule)
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Principal bronchiole. The respiratory unit (respiratory lobule) begins with the respiratory bronchiole and includes structures where gas exchange occurs.

Components of respiratory unit:

  • Respiratory bronchiole ✓

  • Alveolar ducts ✓

  • Atria ✓

  • Alveolar sacs and alveoli ✓

Principal bronchiole ✗

  • It is a conducting airway

  • Does not participate in gas exchange

  • Not included in the respiratory unit

High-yield Respiratory recall:

Part Function
Conducting zone Transport air (no gas exchange)
Respiratory unit Gas exchange
Respiratory bronchiole First site of gas exchange
Alveoli Main site of gas exchange

Exam pearl:
Respiratory unit = respiratory bronchiole + alveolar ducts + atria + alveoli; principal bronchiole is excluded.

Physiology-02.question: ১৩) Pulmonary circulation
১৪) Direct method of measurement of cardiac output
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Fick method. The Fick principle is considered the direct method for measurement of cardiac output because it calculates cardiac output from oxygen consumption and arteriovenous oxygen difference.

Formula:

Cardiac output = O₂ consumption / (Arterial O₂ content − Venous O₂ content)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Indicator method ✗ → An indirect indicator dilution technique.

  • Dye dilution method ✗ → A type of indicator dilution method, not direct.

  • Doppler echocardiography ✗ → Non-invasive indirect estimation of cardiac output.

High-yield Cardiac physiology recall:

Method Type
Fick method Direct measurement of cardiac output
Indicator/dye dilution Indirect
Doppler echo Non-invasive estimation

Exam pearl:
Fick principle = gold standard direct method for cardiac output measurement.

Physiology-02.question: ১৫) Utilization of O2 by tissues is reduced in which form of hypoxia?
১৬) Viscosity is decreased in
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Severe anaemia. Blood viscosity decreases in severe anaemia because the number of red blood cells and haematocrit are reduced.

Factors affecting blood viscosity:

  • ↑ RBC count / haematocrit → ↑ viscosity

  • ↓ RBC count / haematocrit → ↓ viscosity

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Polycythaemia vera (hereditary polycythaemia) ✗ → Increased RBC mass → increased viscosity.

  • Spherocytosis ✗ → Abnormal RBC shape; viscosity is not characteristically decreased.

  • Excess immunoglobulins in blood ✗ → Increases plasma viscosity (hyperviscosity syndrome).

High-yield Blood physiology recall:

Condition Effect on viscosity
Severe anaemia ↓ Viscosity
Polycythaemia ↑ Viscosity
Multiple myeloma (↑ Ig) ↑ Viscosity

Exam pearl:
Anaemia → low haematocrit → low blood viscosity.

Physiology-02.question: ১৭) A person with … frequently has cyanosis?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Polycythaemia. Cyanosis is frequently seen in polycythaemia because increased red cell mass raises the amount of deoxygenated haemoglobin, producing a bluish discoloration of skin and mucous membranes.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Anaemia ✗ → Total haemoglobin is reduced, so cyanosis is usually absent even if oxygen saturation falls.

  • Leukaemia ✗ → Abnormal white cell proliferation; cyanosis is not a typical feature.

  • Purpura ✗ → Due to bleeding tendency (platelet/coagulation defect), causing skin bruising.

High-yield Blood physiology recall:

Condition Effect
Polycythaemia ↑ RBC mass → ↑ viscosity → cyanosis
Anaemia ↓ Hb → pallor
Leukaemia ↑ WBC
Purpura Bleeding into skin

Exam pearl:
Polycythaemia → increased deoxygenated haemoglobin → cyanosis (plethora + bluish discoloration).

Physiology-02.exp: Reference: Guyton 14th; P- 528

Physiology-02.question: ২০) Pulse pressure does not depend on
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Sex. Pulse pressure depends mainly on stroke volume and arterial compliance (elasticity), not on sex.

Formula:

Pulse pressure = Systolic BP − Diastolic BP

Factors affecting pulse pressure:

  • Stroke volume ✓ → ↑ stroke volume → ↑ pulse pressure

  • Arterial elastic constant/compliance ✓ → stiff arteries increase pulse pressure

  • Age ✓ → ageing reduces arterial elasticity → wider pulse pressure

Sex ✗

  • Does not directly determine pulse pressure.

High-yield Cardiovascular recall:

Factor Effect on pulse pressure
↑ Stroke volume ↑ Pulse pressure
↓ Arterial compliance ↑ Pulse pressure
Increased age ↑ Pulse pressure
Sex No significant direct effect

Exam pearl:
Pulse pressure depends on stroke volume and arterial compliance, not sex.

Physiology-02.question: ২১) “When Oxygen Binds With Haemoglobin, CO2 Is Released to increase CO2 Transport”- this effect is called
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Haldane effect. When oxygen binds with haemoglobin in the lungs, it reduces haemoglobin's ability to carry CO₂, causing CO₂ release and increasing CO₂ transport from tissues to lungs.

Mechanism:

  • Oxygenation of Hb → ↓ affinity of Hb for CO₂ and H⁺

  • CO₂ is released from carbaminohaemoglobin

  • Helps removal of CO₂ during expiration

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Bohr effect ✗ → Increased CO₂/H⁺ reduces Hb affinity for O₂, promoting oxygen release to tissues.

  • Chloride shift ✗ → Exchange of HCO₃⁻ and Cl⁻ across RBC membrane during CO₂ transport.

  • Ohm effect ✗ → Related to electrical resistance, not gas transport.

High-yield Respiratory recall:

Effect Main concept
Haldane effect O₂ binding to Hb → CO₂ release
Bohr effect CO₂/H⁺ → O₂ release
Chloride shift HCO₃⁻ movement in RBC

Exam pearl:
Haldane effect = oxygenation of haemoglobin facilitates CO₂ unloading in lungs.

Physiology-02.question: ২২) Obstructive pulmonary disease of upper respiratory tract
২৩) BP on arm is measured over
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Brachial artery. Blood pressure is measured in the upper arm by placing the cuff over the brachial artery, which is the continuation of the axillary artery.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Radial artery ✗ → Used for palpating pulse and arterial blood sampling, not routine BP measurement.

  • Ulnar artery ✗ → Not used for routine BP measurement.

  • Axillary artery ✗ → Proximal artery; not the standard site for arm BP measurement.

High-yield Cardiovascular recall:

BP measurement site:

  • Cuff → Upper arm

  • Stethoscope → Brachial artery

  • Korotkoff sounds → Determine systolic and diastolic pressure

Exam pearl:
Blood pressure in the arm is measured over the brachial artery.

Physiology-02.question: ২৪) Which mainly controls rate and depth of breathing?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Pneumotaxic centre. The pneumotaxic centre in the pons mainly controls the rate and depth of breathing by regulating the duration of inspiration.

Functions:

  • Pneumotaxic centre (pons) → Limits inspiration → controls rate and depth of respiration

  • Strong activity → shorter inspiration → increased respiratory rate

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Dorsal respiratory centre ✗ → Mainly responsible for basic inspiratory rhythm generation.

  • Ventral respiratory centre ✗ → Active mainly during forced breathing.

  • Apneustic centre ✗ → Promotes inspiration and prolongs inspiratory signals.

High-yield Respiratory recall:

Centre Location Function
Pneumotaxic centre Pons Controls rate & depth of breathing
Dorsal respiratory centre Medulla Quiet inspiration
Ventral respiratory centre Medulla Forced inspiration/expiration
Apneustic centre Pons Prolongs inspiration

Exam pearl:
Pneumotaxic centre = “respiratory switch” controlling inspiration duration, rate and depth.

Physiology-02.question: ২৫) Rapidly acting BP regulating mechanisms excludes
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Renal mechanism. Renal regulation of blood pressure is a long-term mechanism and does not act rapidly.

Rapidly acting BP regulatory mechanisms:

  • Baroreceptor mechanism ✓
    → Acts within seconds through autonomic nervous system

  • Chemoreceptor mechanism ✓
    → Responds to changes in O₂, CO₂, and pH

  • CNS ischemic mechanism ✓
    → Powerful emergency response during severe hypotension

  • Renal mechanism ✗
    → Acts slowly through RAAS, sodium balance, and fluid volume regulation

High-yield Cardiovascular recall:

Mechanism Response
Baroreceptor Seconds
Chemoreceptor Seconds–minutes
CNS ischemic response Emergency, rapid
Renal mechanism Long-term (hours–days)

Exam pearl:
Kidney = long-term BP control; baroreceptor = short-term BP control.

Physiology-02.question: ২৬) The ultimate goal of respiration is to maintain proper concentrations of the following in the tissues except?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is NH₃⁻. The ultimate goal of respiration is to maintain normal tissue levels of oxygen, carbon dioxide, and hydrogen ions (pH), but ammonia is not a respiratory gas-regulated substance.

Respiration maintains:

  • O₂ ✓ → Provides oxygen for cellular metabolism

  • CO₂ ✓ → Removes metabolic waste and regulates acid–base balance

  • H⁺ ✓ → Maintains normal pH through CO₂–bicarbonate buffer system

NH₃⁻ ✗

  • Not involved in respiratory regulation.

  • Ammonia is mainly handled by the liver (urea cycle) and kidneys.

High-yield Respiratory recall:

Main goals of respiration:

  1. Maintain adequate O₂

  2. Remove CO₂

  3. Maintain acid–base balance (H⁺ concentration)

Exam pearl:
Respiration regulates O₂, CO₂, and H⁺ — not ammonia.

Physiology-02.question: ২৭) Can be measured by spirometry
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Vital capacity (VC). Spirometry can directly measure lung volumes that involve air movement in and out of the lungs, such as vital capacity.

Spirometry can measure:

  • Vital capacity (VC) ✓

  • Tidal volume (TV)

  • Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV)

  • Expiratory reserve volume (ERV)

Spirometry cannot measure:

  • Residual volume (RV) ✗ → Air remaining after maximum expiration

  • Functional residual capacity (FRC) ✗ → ERV + RV

  • Total lung capacity (TLC) ✗ → VC + RV

High-yield Respiratory recall:

Volume/Capacity Measured by spirometry?
Vital capacity Yes
Residual volume No
Functional residual capacity No
Total lung capacity No

Exam pearl:
Any volume containing RV cannot be measured by simple spirometry.

Physiology-02.question: ২৮) Which are the major sites of resistance of circulation?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Arterioles. Arterioles are the major resistance vessels of the circulatory system because they have a large amount of smooth muscle that can regulate their diameter and blood flow.

Functions:

  • Arterioles regulate:

    • Peripheral vascular resistance

    • Blood pressure

    • Distribution of blood flow to tissues

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Arteries ✗ → Mainly conduct blood; less resistance compared with arterioles.

  • Capillaries ✗ → Major site of exchange of gases and nutrients, but not the main resistance vessels.

  • Veins ✗ → Mainly capacitance vessels (blood storage).

High-yield Cardiovascular recall:

Vessel Main role
Arterioles Major resistance vessels
Capillaries Exchange vessels
Veins Capacitance vessels
Arteries Pressure-conducting vessels

Exam pearl:
Arterioles = “resistance vessels” controlling systemic vascular resistance and BP.

Physiology-02.question: ৩১) Definite cyanosis appears whenever the arterial blood contains more than …. grams of deoxygenated hemoglobin in each 100 ml of blood?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is 5 g. Definite cyanosis appears when arterial blood contains more than approximately 5 g of deoxygenated haemoglobin per 100 mL of blood.

Key point:

  • Cyanosis depends on the absolute amount of deoxygenated Hb, not only oxygen saturation.

  • Threshold: >5 g/dL of reduced haemoglobin → visible cyanosis

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 3 g ✗ → Below the usual threshold for visible cyanosis.

  • 4 g ✗ → Usually insufficient for definite cyanosis.

  • 7 g ✗ → Higher than the accepted threshold.

High-yield Respiratory recall:

Condition Deoxygenated Hb
Visible cyanosis >5 g/100 ml blood
Anaemia Cyanosis may be absent despite low O₂ saturation
Polycythaemia Cyanosis appears more easily

Exam pearl:
Cyanosis appears when reduced Hb exceeds ~5 g/dL.

Physiology-02.question: ৩২) O2-Hb dissociation curve becomes almost flat when PO2 becomes....mmHg?
Physiology-02.exp: Explanation:

Physiology-02.question: ৩৩) Primary expiratory muscle
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Internal intercostal muscles. During forced expiration, internal intercostal muscles contract to depress the ribs and reduce thoracic volume, helping expel air from the lungs.

Functions of respiratory muscles:

  • Internal intercostal muscles ✓
    → Primary muscles of forced expiration

  • Diaphragm ✗
    → Primary muscle of inspiration

  • Sternocleidomastoid ✗
    → Accessory muscle of forced inspiration

  • External intercostal muscles ✗
    → Assist in inspiration by elevating ribs

High-yield Respiratory recall:

Muscle Function
Diaphragm Main muscle of inspiration
External intercostals Inspiration
Internal intercostals Forced expiration
Abdominal muscles Forced expiration

Exam pearl:
Quiet expiration is passive; forced expiration uses internal intercostal muscles.

Physiology-02.question: ৩৬) Maximum % of total blood that can be removed with almost no effect on cardiac output?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is 10%. Approximately 10% of total blood volume can be removed without significant effect on cardiac output due to compensatory mechanisms.

Mechanism:

  • Venous system acts as a blood reservoir

  • Mild blood loss causes:

    • Venoconstriction

    • Increased venous return

    • Maintenance of cardiac output

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 5% ✗ → Too low; smaller than the tolerated amount.

  • 15% ✗ → Begins to produce noticeable haemodynamic changes.

  • 20% ✗ → Significant blood loss causing reduced cardiac output and shock risk.

High-yield Cardiovascular recall:

Blood loss Effect
Up to ~10% Minimal effect on cardiac output
10–20% Compensatory response activated
>20% Reduced cardiac output, shock risk

Exam pearl:
Removal of ~10% blood volume produces little or no change in cardiac output.

Physiology-02.question: ৩৭) Stages of shock excludes
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Indefinite. The classical stages of shock are non-progressive (compensated), progressive, and irreversible stages.

Stages of shock:

  1. Non-progressive stage (Compensated shock) ✓
    → Compensatory mechanisms maintain circulation

  2. Progressive stage ✓
    → Tissue hypoxia worsens and shock becomes self-perpetuating

  3. Irreversible stage ✓
    → Severe cellular injury leading to death despite treatment

Indefinite ✗

  • Not a recognized stage of shock.

High-yield Shock recall:

Stage Feature
Non-progressive Compensation maintains BP
Progressive Worsening hypoperfusion
Irreversible Permanent organ damage

Exam pearl:
Shock stages = Non-progressive → Progressive → Irreversible.

Physiology-02.question: ৩৮) Manifestations of shock includes all of the following except?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is High blood pressure. Shock is characterized by inadequate tissue perfusion and usually causes a fall in blood pressure (hypotension), not hypertension.

Common manifestations of shock:

  • ↓ Cardiac output ✓

  • Rapid, thready pulse (tachycardia) ✓

  • ↑ Respiratory rate (tachypnoea) ✓

  • ↓ Blood pressure ✓ (in most types of shock)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Decrease in cardiac output ✓ → Major feature of shock.

  • Rapid thready pulse ✓ → Due to sympathetic activation.

  • Increase in respiratory rate ✓ → Response to tissue hypoxia.

High-yield Shock recall:

Feature Change in shock
Cardiac output ↓
Blood pressure ↓
Pulse Rapid, weak
Respiratory rate ↑

Exam pearl:
Shock = low perfusion state → ↓ cardiac output + hypotension + tachycardia.

Physiology-02.question: ৩৯) Cardiac output is increased to highest limit in
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Anaemia. Cardiac output increases markedly in severe anaemia as a compensatory mechanism to maintain oxygen delivery to tissues.

Mechanism:

  • ↓ Haemoglobin → ↓ oxygen-carrying capacity

  • Body compensates by:

    • ↑ Heart rate

    • ↑ Stroke volume

    • ↑ Cardiac output

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Beriberi ✗ → Can cause high-output heart failure, but the classical and most significant increase is seen in severe anaemia.

  • MI ✗ → Myocardial damage reduces contractility → ↓ cardiac output.

  • Cardiac shock ✗ → Severe pump failure → markedly ↓ cardiac output.

High-yield Cardiovascular recall:

Condition Effect on cardiac output
Severe anaemia ↑↑ Cardiac output (high-output state)
Beriberi ↑ Cardiac output
MI ↓ Cardiac output
Cardiogenic shock ↓ Cardiac output

Exam pearl:
Anaemia → reduced oxygen delivery → compensatory high cardiac output state.

Physiology-02.question: ৪২) Ventricular depolarisation in ECG is represented by
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is QRS complex. Ventricular depolarisation is represented by the QRS complex on ECG.

ECG components:

  • P wave ✗
    → Atrial depolarisation

  • QRS complex ✓
    → Ventricular depolarisation

  • T wave ✗
    → Ventricular repolarisation

  • ST segment ✗
    → Period when ventricles are fully depolarised (plateau phase)

High-yield ECG recall:

ECG component Represents
P wave Atrial depolarisation
QRS complex Ventricular depolarisation
T wave Ventricular repolarisation
PR interval AV conduction delay

Exam pearl:
QRS = ventricles depolarise and contract.

Physiology-02.question: ৪৩) Tall peaked P wave indicates hypertrophy of
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Right atrium. Tall peaked P waves on ECG indicate right atrial hypertrophy (P pulmonale).

ECG features of atrial enlargement:

  • Right atrial hypertrophy (RAH) ✓
    → Tall, peaked P wave (>2.5 mm in inferior leads)
    → Called P pulmonale

  • Left atrial hypertrophy ✗
    → Broad, notched P wave (P mitrale)

  • Left ventricular hypertrophy ✗
    → Increased QRS voltage

  • Right ventricular hypertrophy ✗
    → Right axis deviation and increased R wave in V1

High-yield ECG recall:

ECG finding Diagnosis
Tall peaked P wave Right atrial hypertrophy (P pulmonale)
Broad notched P wave Left atrial hypertrophy (P mitrale)
High QRS voltage Ventricular hypertrophy

Exam pearl:
P pulmonale = Pulmonary disease → Right atrial enlargement → Tall peaked P wave.

Physiology-02.question: ৪৪) The most important components of surfactant
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine (DPPC). DPPC is the major and most important phospholipid component of pulmonary surfactant, responsible for reducing alveolar surface tension.

Components of surfactant:

  • Dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine (DPPC) ✓ → Major surface tension–reducing component (~60%)

  • Surfactant apoproteins (SP-A, SP-B, SP-C, SP-D) → Help in spreading, stability, and immunity

  • Cholesterol → Minor lipid component

  • Calcium ions → Not a major component

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Surfactant apoproteins ✗ → Important but not the main surface-active component.

  • Calcium ions ✗ → Not a major constituent.

  • Cholesterol ✗ → Present in small amounts.

High-yield Respiratory recall:

Component Role
DPPC Main surface tension–reducing phospholipid
SP-B/SP-C Surfactant spreading
SP-A/SP-D Immune function

Exam pearl:
DPPC (lecithin) = major component of pulmonary surfactant.

Physiology-02.question: ৪৫) Which is usually used to measure cardiac cycle length?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is RR interval. The cardiac cycle length is measured from the beginning of one ventricular depolarisation to the beginning of the next, represented by the interval between two successive R waves (RR interval) on ECG.

ECG intervals:

  • RR interval ✓
    → Duration of one cardiac cycle
    → Used to calculate heart rate

  • PR interval ✗
    → Time from atrial depolarisation to ventricular depolarisation (AV conduction time)

  • QRS complex ✗
    → Duration of ventricular depolarisation

  • ST segment ✗
    → Period of ventricular depolarisation (plateau phase)

High-yield ECG recall:

ECG component Represents
RR interval Cardiac cycle length
PR interval AV conduction time
QRS duration Ventricular depolarisation time
QT interval Total ventricular electrical activity

Exam pearl:
RR interval = time between two heartbeats = duration of one cardiac cycle.

Physiology-02.question: ৪৬) Heart rate may increase in
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Hyperthyroidism. Excess thyroid hormones increase sympathetic activity and metabolic demand, causing tachycardia and increased heart rate.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Parasympathetic stimuli ✗
    → Vagal stimulation decreases SA node firing → ↓ heart rate

  • Fear ✓
    → Actually increases heart rate through sympathetic activation, but the best chronic physiological condition among options is hyperthyroidism.

  • Sleep ✗
    → Increased vagal tone during sleep causes ↓ heart rate

  • Hyperthyroidism ✓
    → ↑ T₃/T₄ → ↑ β-adrenergic sensitivity → ↑ heart rate

High-yield Cardiovascular recall:

Condition Effect on heart rate
Sympathetic stimulation ↑ HR
Fear/exercise ↑ HR
Hyperthyroidism ↑ HR
Parasympathetic stimulation ↓ HR
Sleep ↓ HR

Exam pearl:
Thyrotoxicosis → tachycardia due to increased β-adrenergic sensitivity.

Physiology-02.question: ৪৭) Pathological causes of sinus bradycardia exclude
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Pregnancy. Pregnancy is a physiological condition and usually causes sinus tachycardia, not sinus bradycardia.

Causes of sinus bradycardia include:

  • Hypothyroidism ✓

  • Myocardial infarction (especially inferior MI due to increased vagal tone) ✓

  • Raised intracranial pressure (Cushing response) ✓

Pregnancy ✗

  • Increased blood volume and cardiac demand usually cause increased heart rate.

High-yield ECG recall:

Condition Effect on heart rate
Hypothyroidism ↓ HR
Inferior MI ↓ HR (vagal stimulation)
Raised ICP ↓ HR
Pregnancy ↑ HR (physiological tachycardia)

Exam pearl:
Pregnancy → sinus tachycardia; hypothyroidism → sinus bradycardia.

Physiology-02.question: ৪৮) Which of the following agents or changes has a negative inotropic effect on the heart?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Acetylcholine (ACh). ACh has a negative inotropic effect by reducing myocardial contractility, mainly through M₂ muscarinic receptors in the heart.

Effects of different agents:

  • Acetylcholine (ACh) ✓
    → ↓ Heart rate (negative chronotropic effect)
    → ↓ Atrial contractility (negative inotropic effect)

  • Increased heart rate ✗
    → Usually increases cardiac output; not a primary negative inotropic effect.

  • Sympathetic stimulation ✗
    → β₁ stimulation → ↑ contractility (positive inotropic effect)

  • Norepinephrine ✗
    → β₁ receptor activation → ↑ myocardial contractility (positive inotropic effect)

High-yield Cardiovascular recall:

Agent Effect on contractility
Sympathetic stimulation / Norepinephrine ↑ Inotropy
Acetylcholine (ACh) ↓ Inotropy
Digoxin ↑ Inotropy
Calcium ↑ Inotropy

Exam pearl:
Parasympathetic stimulation via ACh decreases cardiac contractility (negative inotropic effect).

Physiology-02.question: ৪৯) The low-resistance pathways between myocardial cells that allow for the spread of action potentials are the
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Gap junctions. Gap junctions provide low-resistance pathways between cardiac muscle cells, allowing rapid spread of action potentials and synchronized contraction of the myocardium.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • T tubules ✗
    → Carry action potentials deep into cardiac muscle cells and help excitation–contraction coupling.

  • Sarcoplasmic reticulum ✗
    → Stores and releases calcium for muscle contraction.

  • Intercalated disks ✗
    → Specialized junctions connecting cardiac cells; they contain gap junctions and desmosomes, but the low-resistance electrical pathway is specifically the gap junction.

High-yield Cardiac muscle recall:

Structure Function
Gap junctions Electrical coupling between cardiac cells
Desmosomes Mechanical attachment
Intercalated discs Connect adjacent cardiac myocytes
T tubules Excitation–contraction coupling

Exam pearl:
Gap junctions = electrical bridges → rapid conduction of cardiac action potentials.

Physiology-02.question: ৫০) Which of the following is the site of highest airway resistance?
Physiology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Medium-sized bronchi. The highest airway resistance occurs in the medium-sized bronchi because they have a smaller total cross-sectional area compared with numerous small airways.

Key concept:

  • Although individual small bronchioles have a high resistance, they are present in very large numbers, giving them a large total cross-sectional area and therefore low overall resistance.

  • The medium-sized bronchi contribute the greatest resistance to airflow.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Trachea ✗ → Large airway with relatively low resistance.

  • Largest bronchi ✗ → Less resistance due to larger diameter.

  • Smallest bronchi ✗ → Individual resistance is high, but total resistance is low due to many parallel airways.

High-yield Respiratory recall:

Airway Resistance
Trachea Low
Large bronchi Low
Medium-sized bronchi Highest
Small bronchioles Low (many in parallel)

Exam pearl:
Maximum airway resistance = medium-sized bronchi.
